processing: A seed-grown population of tea plants, not a finished tea. Its leaf is considered suited to green tea, made in the usual way by fixing, rolling and drying.
harvest_season: A mid-season plant by bud break; it is picked in spring as is usual for Hubei greens, and exact dates are not recorded.
appearance_dry: Little is recorded; the leaf makes a green tea from small, green shoots, so expect fairly fine, dark green leaf.
appearance_liquor: Typical of Hubei green tea, a clear yellow-green.
appearance_wet: Typical of the class; fresh shoots are small and green and the mature leaf is an elliptical bright green.
taste_profile: Green tea from it is described as fresh-scented and mellow. Seed-grown plants vary, so individual teas may differ more than clonal ones.

brewing.notes: A general starting point for spring green tea. Use cooler water for the finest pickings.

vintage_note: Seldom sold under its own name; the leaf ends up in Yingshan green teas such as Yingshan Yunwu. As with other Chinese greens, these sell as the current spring harvest and are best drunk within the year. A label naming the population is a good sign the seller knows the garden, but ask for the picking date.
description:
Yingshan Qunti is the old local tea population of Yingshan county in the Dabie Mountains of eastern Hubei. Qunti means population: these plants are raised from seed, so one garden holds many slightly different individuals, unlike a clonal cultivar where every bush is a copy.

Botanically it is a shrub with medium-sized leaves and mid-season budding. The bushes are half-spreading and densely branched, with hard, elliptical bright green leaves and small green shoots. It is noted for cold tolerance and fits the tea gardens of eastern Hubei.

A spring sample of one bud and two leaves measured 3.3% amino acids, 24.5% tea polyphenols and 4.9% caffeine. That balance points to a fairly brisk leaf with decent savoury sweetness, and in practice it is used for green tea described as fresh-scented and mellow.

Expect variation. That is the charm of seed-grown tea and also the reason it is hard to promise a flavour. If you find a tea made from it, compare it with a clonal Hubei green from the same spring to see what the diversity does in the cup.
history: It is a traditional local population of Yingshan county, and no breeder or date of origin is recorded, as is normal for seed-grown local tea. Its importance comes through the county's tea industry, which has become the largest by output in Hubei.
